primaryText: Everyone is eating a cheeseburger. It is very large!
discourseSegments: Everyone is eating a cheeseburger.
It is very large!
translation: Everyone is eating a cheeseburger. It is very large!
context: Everyone is (atypically) sharing a huge cheeseburger.

alternatives.form: Everyone is eating a cheeseburger. They are very large!

comment: A summation pronoun referring to the totality of cheeseburgers being eaten; singular or plural by the cardinality of its antecedent description.

primaryText: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. It is very large!
discourseSegments: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger.
It is very large!
translation: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. It is very large!

alternatives.form: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. They are very large!

readings.name: the burger she might be eating is/would be large

primaryText: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. They are on the kitchen counter.
discourseSegments: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger.
They are on the kitchen counter.
translation: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. They are on the kitchen counter.

readings.name: the various cheeseburgers Andrea might be eating are all on the counter

comment: Summation pronouns never operate over multiple worlds at once.

primaryText: There might already be a winner in the mayoral election. She is a woman.
discourseSegments: There might already be a winner in the mayoral election.
She is a woman.
translation: There might already be a winner in the mayoral election. She is a woman.
context: Exactly five well-known candidates have run, no write-ins; late on election night the speaker has not checked the news, and may even have one candidate in mind as the possible winner.

alternatives.form: There might already be a winner in the mayoral election. They are women.

readings.name: the possible winner is a woman

comment: The candidates exist in every world of the context set, so existence of the referents does not license the pronoun; the antecedent description 'winner' is empty in some context-set worlds.

primaryText: If there's a light on at 9pm, it is possible that one of the teachers is still inside the school building. She is working late.
discourseSegments: If there's a light on at 9pm, it is possible that one of the teachers is still inside the school building.
She is working late.
translation: If there's a light on at 9pm, it is possible that one of the teachers is still inside the school building. She is working late.
context: The teachers of a particular school; the speaker has no particular teacher in mind.

primaryText: There must be some sort of animal in the shed. It's making quite a racket!
discourseSegments: There must be some sort of animal in the shed.
It's making quite a racket!
translation: There must be some sort of animal in the shed. It's making quite a racket!
comment: Epistemic 'must' is realistic: the antecedent description has a unique extension in every world of the context set, the actual one included.

primaryText: If it's cancer, there must be a test. — You just did it.
discourseSegments: JASON: If it's cancer, there must be a test.
HOUSE: You just did it.
translation: If it's cancer, there must be a test. — You just did it.

primaryText: Jerry might own a car, but they are still a hassle.
translation: Jerry might own a car, but they are still a hassle.

alternatives.form: Jerry doesn't own a car—they are too much of a hassle!

comment: Kind reference is scopeless and is set aside from the intensional cases.

primaryText: A dog appeared. It barked.
discourseSegments: A dog appeared.
It barked.
translation: A dog appeared. It barked.
comment: The indefinite is a local variable, the pronoun the same variable, and the discourse the closure of their conjunction.

primaryText: Between one and five bunnies live in my yard. It ate my tulips.
discourseSegments: Between one and five bunnies live in my yard.
It ate my tulips.
translation: Between one and five bunnies live in my yard. It ate my tulips.
comment: In some worlds the antecedent denotes a non-singleton plurality, so the first sentence does not entail the singular pronoun's presupposition.

primaryText: Every farmer that owns a donkey beats it.
translation: Every farmer that owns a donkey beats it.
comment: The nuclear scope is subordinate to the restriction, whose bracketed donkey variable licenses the pronoun.

primaryText: Every farmer that owns a donkey beats it. Most treat it well otherwise.
discourseSegments: Every farmer that owns a donkey beats it.
Most treat it well otherwise.
translation: Every farmer that owns a donkey beats it. Most treat it well otherwise.

readings.name: most of the donkeys that are owned and beaten are otherwise treated well

comment: Quantificational subordination: the implicit restriction of 'most' is the nuclear scope of the previous quantifier.

primaryText: If Sal has a pet, it must be a donkey.
translation: If Sal has a pet, it must be a donkey.
comment: A conditional donkey sentence: the nuclear scope of the modal is subordinate to its if-clause restriction.

primaryText: A wolf might enter. It would eat Tasty Tim.
discourseSegments: A wolf might enter.
It would eat Tasty Tim.
translation: A wolf might enter. It would eat Tasty Tim.
comment: Roberts's modal subordination: the null restriction of 'would' is anaphoric to the nuclear scope of 'might'.

primaryText: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
discourseSegments: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria.
They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
translation: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
comment: A simple pronoun need not exhaust its antecedent description.

primaryText: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
discourseSegments: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria.
They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
translation: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.
comment: A summation pronoun denotes the complete set satisfying the nuclear scope, leaving nothing for 'other girls'.

primaryText: Almost every girl brought in the paper she wrote. Few of them forgot it at home.
discourseSegments: Almost every girl brought in the paper she wrote.
Few of them forgot it at home.
translation: Almost every girl brought in the paper she wrote. Few of them forgot it at home.

readings.name: 'it' refers to the papers written by the few forgetful girls

comment: A paycheck pronoun: the antecedent description contains a free variable bound by a different operator at the pronoun.

primaryText: Andrea is eating a cheeseburger. It is large.
discourseSegments: Andrea is eating a cheeseburger.
It is large.
translation: Andrea is eating a cheeseburger. It is large.
comment: The first sentence asserts the singularity the pronoun presupposes.

primaryText: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. It is large.
discourseSegments: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger.
It is large.
translation: Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger. It is large.
comment: Among the worlds where Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger are ones where she is fasting; there the summation is empty and the singular presupposition fails.

primaryText: There may already be a winner in the mayoral race. She is a woman, you know.
discourseSegments: There may already be a winner in the mayoral race.
She is a woman, you know.
translation: There may already be a winner in the mayoral race. She is a woman, you know.
context: A known set of real-life candidates, no write-ins; late on election night the tabulation might be over.

readings.name: the likely/possible/potential winner is a woman

primaryText: Hob thinks a witch has blighted Bob's mare, and Nob wonders whether she (the same witch) killed Cob's sow.
translation: Hob thinks a witch has blighted Bob's mare, and Nob wonders whether she (the same witch) killed Cob's sow.
context: A town with an outbreak of witch mania.
comment: Descriptivist analysis: the pronoun is felicitous where every world Nob considers has one witch who blighted the mare.

primaryText: Either there's no bathroom in this house or it's in a funny place.
translation: Either there's no bathroom in this house or it's in a funny place.

alternatives.form: Either John doesn't own a donkey, or he keeps it very quiet.

comment: Attributed to Barbara Partee in Roberts 1987; felicity reduces to 'if there is a bathroom there is exactly one', the scalar implicature of singular 'no bathroom'.
